title: How to plot a land title technical description | Spatialdom Insights
description: A practical reading workflow for plotting bearings and distances from a Philippine land title, checking closure, and knowing when to ask a geodetic engineer.
heading: How to plot a land title technical description
intro: A plot turns a list of boundary calls into a shape you can inspect. Start with the source document, follow the lines in order, and treat any mismatch as a question to investigate.

sections.heading: Prepare the source
paragraphs: Use a legible technical description and, if available, the approved survey plan. Record the lot and plan identifiers, the point of beginning, each line's bearing and distance, and the unit shown. Keep the source beside the plot so every entry can be checked.

Separate the tie line from the parcel boundary. A tie point helps locate the lot relative to a reference; the boundary calls describe the lot's shape. Drawing only the boundary can help you understand the shape, but it does not establish its position on the ground.

sections.heading: Trace and check the lines
paragraphs: Begin at the first lot corner. Enter each bearing and distance in the order written, moving from the end of one line to the start of the next. Check the quadrant letters, degrees, minutes, seconds, decimal places, and units before proceeding.

After the final line, compare the drawing with the plan and check whether the path returns to its starting point. If it does not, first recheck transcription, omitted lines, and point order. A mismatch in a quick plot is not proof that the title or survey is wrong.

sections.heading: Know what the plot can answer
paragraphs: A plot can expose an unexpected shape or a line that deserves a closer look. It cannot confirm ownership, title validity, physical monuments, or an official boundary. For a decision about a property, compare the relevant official records and ask a licensed geodetic engineer to review material discrepancies.
